case_study_insert.main_stem: Arden Automotive Components (AAC) is a public limited company in the automotive components sector, manufacturing brake caliper assemblies and suspension brackets for car manufacturers, employing a workforce of 340. Founded in 1998 by Sunita Rao, AAC operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. AAC plans to invest $2,300,000 in relocating its press shop to a new industrial park with expanded capacity, financed by a $1,200,000 bank loan and a $1,100,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $570,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.80 a unit and a selling price of $15.50, and currently produces 150,000 units a year. AAC faces an HR problem: labour turnover has risen to 14% and qualified welders are scarce.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — October 2026: AAC's press shop produced 12,400 brake caliper assemblies last month, with a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.4% a year ago. On-time delivery to car manufacturers was 91%. Labour turnover reached 14% in the welding department, and 7% of shifts were short-staffed. Planned capacity after the move is 16,000 units a month. A workforce survey of 120 employees found 62% want overtime paid at a premium rate, and 48% feel underpaid relative to rival plants. On-the-job training is the current approach; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $1,400 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Arden Automotive Components as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.9% to 5.6%, increasing costs for AAC's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $11.12 to $11.80 per hour from April 2027. (3) Aluminium and steel input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, vehicle production inflation is running at 5.9%, while consumer demand for new cars grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: AAC plans to finance the industrial park relocation partly with a share issue. Explain two advantages for AAC of using a share issue instead of taking on a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no repayments and no interest, protecting AAC's cash flow while it funds the $2,300,000 relocation and services a $1,200,000 bank loan. Every dollar not committed to interest can cushion the 11.2% rise in aluminium and steel input costs instead of forcing a price increase above the $15.50 selling price paid by car manufacturers.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the relocation risk across many public investors and strengthens liquidity at a time when AAC holds current liabilities of $900,000 in 2025, rather than concentrating repayment pressure in a single lender. It also avoids further collateral demands on the new industrial park press shop, though existing shareholders' control is diluted and dividends per share may fall until the relocated capacity ramps up to 16,000 units a month. This trade-off suits a public limited company able to tap capital markets when a bank loan alone would strain its workforce of 340 and its 14% labour turnover problem.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Arden Automotive Components and its relocation decision.

questions.question_text: AAC is relaunching after the relocation. Consider exhibiting at a major automotive trade fair, advertising in automotive industry journals, or a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at car manufacturers. Which should AAC choose to promote its brake caliper assemblies? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade fair exhibiting: A major automotive exhibition puts AAC's brake caliper assemblies directly in front of purchasing engineers from car manufacturers, allows live demonstrations of the relocated press shop's automated lines and can yield multi-year contracts. However, stand space, travel and staffing are very expensive, one event every few months cannot sustain momentum for 150,000 units a year, and conversations may not convert quickly.

Journal advertising: Automotive industry journals reach exactly the engineers and buyers AAC wants, and print advertisements build credibility and repetition across issues at a fraction of broadcast costs. Readership is passive, response is hard to measure, and lead times are long, so journal advertising supports brand awareness but rarely wins a contract on its own.

LinkedIn campaign: A targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement engineers in the car manufacturing sector scales nationally, is measurable click by click and is far cheaper per contact than either alternative. It can showcase the 91% on-time delivery record and 2.2% defect rate that justify AAC's premium over rivals, though it requires skilled content creation and rapid follow-up to turn interest into orders.

Recommendation: AAC should choose a targeted LinkedIn campaign, backed by one flagship trade fair each year. It reaches the exact decision-makers at low cost, feeds the relocated capacity of 16,000 units a month and supports the democratic, consultative image Sunita Rao wants after the move. Journal advertising is rejected as too passive to generate contracts, and exhibiting alone is rejected as too infrequent and expensive for a 340-person manufacturer already servicing a $1,200,000 bank loan and a $2,300,000 relocation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AAC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AAC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and exhibition-only approaches are rejected.

questions.question_text: AAC's labour turnover has risen to 14% in the welding department. Explain two benefits for AAC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its welders.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives AAC's welders a genuine voice in how shifts, overtime rotas and welding procedures are arranged, which satisfies esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Welders who help design rotas are far more likely to stay, directly attacking the 14% labour turnover that is forcing AAC to recruit scarce replacements and disrupting the 12,400 assemblies produced each month.

Point 2: Involving welders in decisions surfaces practical ideas from the people who handle every brake caliper daily, improving weld quality and helping push the defect rate below 2.2%. Higher commitment and sense of ownership also raise output towards the planned 16,000 units a month at the new industrial park, saving the $1,400 per employee cost of off-the-job certification every time a welder leaves and protecting on-time delivery to car manufacturers. Democratic consultation also signals respect for welders, which matters when 48% of the surveyed workforce feels underpaid relative to rival plants and turnover is already 14%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AAC's labour turnover, quality and relocation.

questions.question_text: AAC must address its shortage of qualified welders. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should AAC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training welders beside experienced staff at the press shop is directly relevant to AAC's brake caliper assemblies, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the line running while staff learn, which protects the 12,400 units produced last month and the 91% on-time delivery record. Drawbacks are that experienced welders lose productive time as mentors, bad habits can be passed on, and certification is informal, which troubles car manufacturers who audit supplier competence.

Off-the-job training: The regional college welding certification costs $1,400 per employee; if we assume 25 of the 340 staff are welders needing certification, that is $35,000, affordable beside a $2,300,000 relocation. Participants gain structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate, strengthening contract bids. However, staff are removed from the line for days at a time, worsening the 7% of short-staffed shifts, and the college content may not perfectly match AAC's exact jigs and tolerances, so follow-up coaching on site would still be needed. Certification also helps AAC defend its contracts when car manufacturers audit supplier competence.

Decision: AAC should choose on-the-job training for the majority of its welders, with off-the-job certification reserved for the most promising leads who can then train others. This keeps output stable while labour turnover is 14%, costs far less than certifying everyone at $1,400, and directly targets the skills gap on its own machines. Full off-the-job training is rejected for now because withdrawing those 25 welders (on that assumption) from a 340-person workforce during a relocation would undermine on-time delivery to car manufacturers and the launch of the new industrial park. AAC should review weld quality and defect rates monthly afterwards, shifting any remaining welders onto college courses once the press shop relocation has settled.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to AAC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of AAC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of AAC with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and contract requirements.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AAC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $570,000 ÷ ($15.50 − $9.80) = $570,000 ÷ $5.70 = 100,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 100,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.50 − $9.80 = $5.70. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.70.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AAC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 100,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 150,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 50,000 units, judging how much room the relocation has before the new industrial park press shop becomes unprofitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.70 lets AAC test a discount to win a rival car manufacturer's contract; a 5% price cut to $14.73 would drop contribution to $4.93, showing how many extra assemblies are needed to keep the $570,000 fixed costs covered.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $570,000 and contribution per unit helps managers check the relocated plant can service the $1,200,000 bank loan before AAC commits to further borrowing for the $2,300,000 move.
4. Managers can use average total cost ($570,000 ÷ 150,000 units + $9.80 = $13.60 a unit) to benchmark quarterly performance, identify waste in the welding department and renegotiate aluminium and steel supply as input costs rise 11.2%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 100,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.70 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 50,000 units versus 150,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $570,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $2,300,000 relocation; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.60 to tackle labour turnover and 11.2% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AAC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has AAC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.39 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.73 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.97 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $500,000 inventories + $550,000 trade receivables + $150,000 cash = $1,200,000; 2025 current assets = $380,000 + $640,000 + $230,000 = $1,250,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $1,200,000 ÷ $960,000 = 1.25; 2025 = $1,250,000 ÷ $900,000 = 1.39. Cover excluding inventories 2024 = ($1,200,000 − $500,000) ÷ $960,000 = $700,000 ÷ $960,000 = 0.73; 2025 = ($1,250,000 − $380,000) ÷ $900,000 = $870,000 ÷ $900,000 = 0.97.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved, though from a weak base. Short-term cover strengthened from 1.25 to 1.39 as inventories were reduced from $500,000 to $380,000 and cash rose to $230,000 while liabilities eased from $960,000 to $900,000. The tougher measure excluding inventories rose from 0.73 to 0.97, so AAC is much less dependent on selling stock to meet short-term debts, which matters while it services a $1,200,000 bank loan for the $2,300,000 relocation. However, trade receivables climbed from $550,000 to $640,000; if car manufacturers stretch payment terms, the stronger position could weaken. The exclude-inventory measure also remains below 1.00, so a demand shock would still pressure AAC.

Conclusion: AAC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.25 to 1.39 and 0.73 to 0.97), and the gains do not rest on stock. The main residual risks are rising receivables and an exclude-inventory measure still under 1.00, so AAC should tighten credit control with car manufacturers and keep building cash before the relocation completes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether AAC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AAC of relocating its press shop to the new industrial park.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The new industrial park gives AAC modern, larger premises with expanded capacity of 16,000 units a month, allowing it to chase larger contracts from car manufacturers and spread the $2,300,000 fixed investment over more output, lowering unit cost. Purpose-built floor space also improves material flow from raw steel to finished brake caliper assemblies, helping sustain the 2.2% defect rate and 91% on-time delivery while easing the shortage of welding space that contributed to congestion and 7% short-staffed shifts. It also positions AAC to win consolidated supply contracts from car manufacturers eager to shorten supply chains after recent disruption.

Disadvantage: Relocation risks serious disruption. Moving heavy presses could halt production for weeks, threatening the 91% on-time delivery record and risking penalties from car manufacturers just as labour turnover is already 14%. The $2,300,000 cost also raises fixed-cost pressure before the expanded capacity generates revenue, and any overrun would strain cash while AAC services its $1,200,000 bank loan and competes against rival plants for the same car manufacturer contracts.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AAC's relocation, capacity and customer commitments.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.6%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect AAC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.9% to 5.6%): A 0.7% rise on AAC's $1,200,000 variable-rate loan adds about $8,400 a year to interest costs and slightly raises the burden above its $570,000 fixed costs. Higher rates may also make car manufacturers more cautious about committing to large contracts, and could increase the cost of future borrowing for the $2,300,000 relocation. The impact is real but modest and can be capped by fixing the rate for part of the loan.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $11.80 per hour): AAC employs 340 staff; if the lowest-paid 45 operatives move from $11.12 to $11.80, each gains about $1,360 a year, or roughly $61,200 across the group. Skilled welders and engineers earn well above the minimum, but with 48% of surveyed employees feeling underpaid relative to rival plants, AAC also faces pressure to raise other wages or risk further rises in labour turnover beyond 14%.

Input cost inflation (11.2% aluminium and steel): Metals dominate AAC's $9.80 variable cost, at roughly $6 of materials per assembly. An 11.2% rise adds about $0.67 per unit; at 150,000 units that is roughly $100,800 a year, directly cutting the $5.70 contribution per unit and squeezing the $15.50 selling price agreed with car manufacturers.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in aluminium and steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeatedly reduces contribution on every unit sold, totalling roughly $100,800 a year, the largest single cash exposure of the three. The wage increase is the second concern at roughly $61,200 a year, compounded by morale risk, while the interest-rate rise costs only about $8,400 a year and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require AAC to negotiate price recovery with car manufacturers and drive down the 2.2% defect rate to protect margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AAC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AAC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AAC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
